descriptor: Burning biomass indoors for cooking and heat: pollutants and a resulting illness, a practical mitigation, why under-five children are more at risk, then sources and exposure controls for two of asbestos, radon, mold.
solution:
**(a)(i)** Any two indoor combustion pollutants: carbon monoxide, particulate matter (soot), nitrogen oxides, sulfur oxides, volatile organic compounds, methane, or trace metals. *(2 points: 1 each)*
**(a)(ii)** Link one pollutant to a named respiratory illness: fine particulates to COPD, asthma, bronchitis or lung cancer; CO to carbon monoxide poisoning. *(1 point: specific illness matched to a pollutant you listed)*
**(b)** Pair an approach with its health effect, e.g. a chimney or vented stove sends smoke outdoors, so less is inhaled; a cleaner, more efficient stove burns less fuel and releases fewer pollutants; switching to biogas, solar or electric cooking removes the smoke source; cooking outdoors moves the smoke away from the home. *(2 points: realistic approach; how it lowers respiratory illness)*
**(c)** Young children breathe in more air per kilogram of body mass, have immature immune systems and narrow airways, and spend more time indoors near the stove, so the dose and effect are larger. *(1 point: one valid reason)*
**(d)** Choose two: asbestos source = old insulation, floor tiles, cement or ceiling products; control = leave undisturbed, seal or enclose, or have it professionally removed. Radon source = uranium-bearing soil and rock whose gas seeps through foundations; control = seal cracks and install subfloor venting. Mold source = leaks, flooding or damp, poorly ventilated rooms; control = fix the leak, dry or ventilate the space, clean or replace damaged material. *(4 points: a source and a control for each of two pollutants)*

descriptor: Piping plover nesting on Assateague Island (two nest maps): preferred habitat, nest change, cause, protecting nests, barrier-island functions, a human threat to coastal habitat, and economic effects of and local defenses against sea-level rise.
solution:
**(a)(i)** Open, unvegetated sandy beach and storm-washover areas. *(1 point)*
**(a)(ii)** Nests fell from 44 in 1999 to 25 in 2009, a drop of about 43%. *(1 point: direction plus a number or percent)*
**(a)(iii)** Plant cover spread over formerly bare sand, so the open sandy nesting habitat shrank. *(1 point: habitat loss from revegetation)*
**(b)(i)** Fence or sign off nesting zones, cover nests with protective enclosures, restrict vehicles, kites or fireworks, or require leashed pets. *(1 point: one realistic restriction)*
**(b)(ii)** Barrier islands absorb wave energy and wind, which reduces mainland erosion and storm-surge flooding; their lagoons and marshes also trap sediment and shelter nursery habitat. *(1 point: one function with its protective effect)*
**(b)(iii)** E.g. beachfront development removes habitat; or trash and plastic entangle or are swallowed by wildlife; or oil spills coat marine life. Name the action and its effect on a species other than the plover. *(2 points: action; effect on species)*
**(c)** Lost tourism revenue, lower property values, repair costs for damaged infrastructure, higher insurance, or loss of farmland or fisheries income. *(1 point: one economic impact)*
**(d)** Two of: raise buildings; set new construction back from the shore; install pumps; build seawalls or groins; plant shoreline vegetation; nourish beaches with sand. *(2 points: 1 each)*
notes: Maps are images in the source; values (44 and 25 nests) come from the scoring guideline.

descriptor: Oil-sands (bitumen) mining under boreal forest in Alberta: forest benefits, environmental costs of extraction and transport, and three unit-conversion calculations (days and years to extract 73 billion barrels; water needed for synthetic crude).
solution:
**(a)** One ecological service: carbon dioxide uptake, climate and water regulation, erosion control, nutrient cycling, soil formation or maintaining biodiversity. *(1 point)*
**(b)** One economic benefit: timber and other forest products, tourism and recreation jobs, or lower health costs from cleaner air. *(1 point)*
**(c)** Two non-habitat consequences: fossil-fuel combustion for machinery and processing releases CO₂, NOₓ, SO₂ and particulates; toxic tailings need storage; spills or leaks from pipelines contaminate water; strip mining adds sediment to streams; large volumes of water are withdrawn. *(2 points: 1 each)*
**(d)** Days = 73 × 10⁹ barrels ÷ (1 × 10⁶ barrels/day) = 7.3 × 10⁴ days = 73,000 days. *(2 points: setup; answer)*
**(e)** Years = 7.3 × 10⁴ days ÷ 365 days/year ≈ 200 years (2 × 10²). *(2 points; an error carried from (d) is not penalized again)*
**(f)** 30 × 10⁶ barrels synthetic crude/month × 2 barrels water/barrel × 12 months/year = 7.2 × 10⁸ barrels of freshwater per year. *(2 points: setup; answer)*

descriptor: Graph of Mauna Loa atmospheric CO₂ and nearby ocean pH since 1992: read values for 2005, relate CO₂ to ocean CO₂ and pH, write the reaction with water, name the problem, explain harm to shell-builders, and name another reef threat.
solution:
**(a)(i)** About 380 ppm CO₂ in 2005 (±5). *(1 point)*
**(a)(ii)** About pH 8.08 in 2005 (±0.02). *(1 point)*
**(b)(i)** More atmospheric CO₂ means more CO₂ dissolves in the ocean. *(1 point)*
**(b)(ii)** Inverse relationship: as atmospheric CO₂ climbs, ocean pH falls (more acidic). *(1 point)*
**(b)(iii)** CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid), which ionizes to H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. *(1 point: balanced equation)*
**(b)(iv)** Ocean acidification. *(1 point)*
**(c)(i)** Added H⁺ lowers the carbonate available and can dissolve calcium carbonate, so shells and coral skeletons form more slowly or erode; weaker organisms have lower reproduction and survival and are easier prey. *(2 points: chemical effect on shell or skeleton; consequence for survival)*
**(c)(ii)** E.g. warming causes bleaching (loss of symbiotic algae); nutrient runoff drives algal blooms that block light and deplete oxygen; destructive fishing or tourism physically breaks reefs; invasive species outcompete natives. *(2 points: threat; how it damages reefs)*
notes: Graph not available as text; the 380 ppm and 8.08 readings are from the guideline.

descriptor: Visibility loss in four national parks (graph): worst park, primary versus secondary pollutants and how each enters or forms, percent increase in Great Smoky Mountains visibility, two government actions, and two non-air impacts of heavy visitation.
solution:
**(a)** Sequoia National Park shows the largest loss of visibility versus the natural baseline. *(1 point)*
**(b)(i)** Primary pollutant example: SO₂, NOₓ, CO, particulate matter or VOCs. *(1 point)*
**(b)(ii)** Primary pollutants enter the air directly from a source such as a smokestack, tailpipe or burning fuel. *(1 point)*
**(b)(iii)** Secondary pollutant example: ozone, sulfuric acid, nitric acid or PANs. *(1 point)*
**(b)(iv)** Secondary pollutants form when primary pollutants react in the air, e.g. NOₓ and VOCs react in sunlight to make ozone, or SO₂ and water form sulfuric acid. *(1 point)*
**(c)(i)** Percent increase = (45 mi − 25 mi) ÷ 25 mi × 100 = 80%. *(1 point)*
**(c)(ii)** Two actions: tighten emission standards or cap-and-trade for utilities; incentivize renewable energy; limit private vehicles with shuttles or parking fees; support electric vehicles; restrict campfires or burning. *(2 points: 1 each)*
**(d)** Two non-air impacts: litter harming wildlife or water; trampling and off-trail travel causing erosion and compaction; roads and facilities fragmenting habitat; noise or light disrupting animal behavior; visitors bringing invasive species; wastewater pollution. *(2 points: 1 each)*
notes: The 2015 Great Smoky Mountains value of 45 miles is read from the graph via the guideline.

descriptor: Homeowner designs a test of rooftop solar panel compass direction (variables, hypothesis, extra variable), then hydroelectric dam diagram: turbine energy step, stored potential energy, pairing with solar or wind, climate risks, reservoir benefit and silt effect.
solution:
**(a)(i)** Independent variable: the compass direction the panels face. *(1)*
**(a)(ii)** Dependent variable: electricity produced (kWh). *(1)*
**(a)(iii)** E.g. "If panels face south (north hemisphere), then they will generate more kWh than panels facing other directions." A null statement of no effect is also acceptable. *(1: testable prediction relating the two variables)*
**(a)(iv)** An uncontrolled variable such as panel tilt, shading, dust or snow, cloud cover, season, or panel temperature. *(1)*
**(b)(i)** The turbine, where moving water's kinetic energy becomes rotational mechanical energy. *(1)*
**(b)(ii)** Water held high behind the dam has gravitational potential energy; releasing it downhill (greater head, more pressure) converts that energy to motion. *(1)*
**(b)(iii)** Solar and wind output varies with weather and time of day; hydro can be dispatched to fill gaps, and surplus solar or wind power can pump water back uphill into the reservoir. *(1)*
**(b)(iv)** Drought, evaporation or reduced snowpack lowers reservoir storage and generation; heavy storms increase sediment that shrinks storage; glacier loss first raises then lowers flow. *(1)*
**(c)(i)** Benefit besides power: flood control, water supply or irrigation, recreation, or lake habitat. *(1)*
**(c)(ii)** Silt reduces storage volume and the head available, lowering output, and abrasion damages turbine blades, raising repair cost. *(1)*

descriptor: Pesticide use in cotton: human-health benefit, exposure route, a 1960-2015 table of application rate versus pests trapped, evidence of resistance, effects on non-target wildlife, crop rotation, a lower-pesticide alternative and its human benefit.
solution:
**(a)** Pesticides suppress disease vectors (mosquitoes, ticks, rodents) and raise food supply, improving health. *(1)*
**(b)** Entry routes: inhaling spray, drinking contaminated water, eating residues on food, or absorption through skin. *(1)*
**(c)(i)** 1975, when only 2 pests were captured. *(1)*
**(c)(ii)** Pests started at 700 (no pesticide), crashed to 2 after first use, then climbed steadily to 1,100 by 2015. *(1)*
**(c)(iii)** Even with the dose rising from 500 to 1,000 g/ha, catches rose from 2 to 1,100: survivors carried heritable resistance and reproduced, so each generation tolerates more pesticide (the pesticide treadmill). *(1)*
**(d)** Two non-lethal effects: contamination of soil and water; bioaccumulation and biomagnification; endocrine disruption and reproductive problems; thinner eggshells; impaired bee signaling; loss of food supply or predators upsetting the food web. *(2: 1 each)*
**(e)(i)** Rotation means growing different crops in sequence on the same field. *(1)*
**(e)(ii)** Integrated pest management, intercropping, timing application to the vulnerable stage, or pest-resistant crop varieties. *(1)*
**(e)(iii)** Justification: less pesticide residue in food, lower input cost and higher farm profit, or fewer exposed workers. *(1)*

descriptor: Subdivision planned on forest used by wood thrush: why specialists suffer from fragmentation, cowbird relationship, benefits of keeping forest, a mitigation proposal, and area and percentage calculations for a 275-territory target.
solution:
**(a)** Specialists have narrow niches, low adaptability and often small, genetically limited populations, so losing or splitting habitat harms them more than flexible generalists. *(1)*
**(b)** Brood parasitism (cowbird benefits, thrush harmed). *(1)*
**(c)** Retained forest keeps some species, reduces erosion, provides shade and transpiration cooling, and can buffer edge effects. *(1)*
**(d)** E.g. wildlife corridors, conservation easements, buffer zones, offsetting preserved land, clustered or vertical housing, shared green space. *(1)*
**(e)** Area = 275 territories × 800 m²/territory = 220,000 m². *(2: setup; answer)*
**(f)** Set-aside = 1,000 lots × 1,100 m² × 0.10 = 110,000 m²; ÷ 800 m² = 137.5 (about 137) territories. *(2)*
**(g)** Needed fraction = 220,000 m² ÷ (1,000 × 1,100 m² = 1,100,000 m²) × 100 = 20% of each lot (twice the developer's 10%). *(2)*

descriptor: Soil erosion rate versus slope for four farming practices (graph), then a road-construction test of straw bales versus grass for sediment control (hypothesis, control, variables, turbidity data), and fish that lay eggs in streambed gravel.
solution:
**(a)(i)** Question: how do slope and land-use or tillage practice (crop rotation, no-till, cover crops) affect annual soil erosion? *(1)*
**(a)(ii)** Crop rotation is the practice that stays within tolerable loss on a 15% slope. *(1)*
**(a)(iii)** A cover crop gives lower erosion than no-till alone, allowing steeper land to stay within the tolerable limit. *(1)*
**(a)(iv)** Natural erosion agents: running water, rainfall or wind. *(1)*
**(b)(i)** Dependent variable: amount of sediment run-off or discharge. *(1)*
**(b)(ii)** Add an untreated bare plot, or measure sediment before and after treatment. *(1)*
**(b)(iii)** An uncontrolled factor: slope, rainfall amount, soil type, plot size, distance to stream, road material or time since rain. *(1)*
**(b)(iv)** Turbidity was measured as sight depth: straw plot 12 cm, grass plot 28 cm. Deeper sight depth means clearer water, so grass trapped more sediment and the hypothesis (straw is better) is rejected. *(1)*
**(c)(i)** Type III: very high early mortality, few survive to adulthood. *(1)*
**(c)(ii)** Sediment smothers eggs and cuts oxygen, removes spawning gravel, carries toxins, warms water (less dissolved oxygen) or clouds water, impairing reproduction. *(1)*

descriptor: Global amphibian species-richness map: richest latitudes, biome and why, a cause of deforestation, richness and resilience, other causes of decline, a species-protection law, and a development plan that protects frogs in a wetland.
solution:
**(a)(i)** Greatest richness lies between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn (roughly 30° N-30° S). *(1)*
**(a)(ii)** Tropical rainforest. *(1)*
**(a)(iii)** Warm, wet conditions all year and high productivity supply many niches, food and habitat. *(1)*
**(b)** Clearing land for farming, housing, fuel or timber. *(1)*
**(c)(i)** A species-rich ecosystem is more resilient: some species survive a stressor and help restore function. *(1)*
**(c)(ii)** Other drivers: pesticide or drug pollution and endocrine disruptors, climate-driven loss of moist habitat, illegal collection, invasive species, habitat fragmentation, chytrid fungus. *(1)*
**(d)(i)** Endangered Species Act, CITES or the Lacey Act. *(1)*
**(d)(ii)** ESA: lists species, bans harming them, protects critical habitat and requires recovery plans; CITES: regulates or bans international trade; Lacey Act: bans trade in illegally taken wildlife. *(1)*
**(e)(i)** E.g. relocate frogs, reserve part of the wetland, build corridors, require a setback, or cluster buildings. *(1)*
**(e)(ii)** Justify with a non-frog benefit, e.g. buffer strip filters runoff, preserve raises rental appeal, clustering frees land and limits fragmentation. *(1)*

descriptor: Replacing aging coal plants with natural gas: why coal is nonrenewable, environmental and economic gains of gas, preventing CO poisoning, then percent change in PM2.5, kilograms of PM2.5 no longer removed by logging, and added hospital admissions.
solution:
**(a)** Coal forms far more slowly than it is burned, so the supply is finite. *(1)*
**(b)** Gas emits less CO₂, no mercury or other trace metals, less NOₓ, SOₓ and particulates, and avoids strip-mining. *(1)*
**(c)** Economic edge: cheaper pipeline transport, fewer pollution controls, cheaper waste disposal, higher plant efficiency or lower health-care costs. *(1)*
**(d)** Install CO detectors, maintain and vent furnaces, mandate detectors, run public education, or change heating system. *(1)*
**(e)** Percent change = (188 − 85) ÷ 85 × 100 = +121% (the table gives 85 for 1990 and 188 for 2016). *(2)*
**(f)** Lost removal = (50,000 − 43,000) ha × 2.3 kg/ha = 7,000 × 2.3 = 16,100 kg PM2.5 per year. *(2)*
**(g)** A 23% rise ÷ 10% = 2.3 steps × 1% = 2.3% increase; 7,390 × 0.023 ≈ 170 additional admissions. *(2)*

descriptor: Snapping-turtle nests upstream and downstream of a mercury-emitting factory (nest map): best site, dependent variable, research question, role of upstream sites, effect of removing bank vegetation, mercury effects, methylmercury origin, claim testing, farming and soil.
solution:
**(a)(i)** Area A (upstream, no mercury). *(1)*
**(a)(ii)** Nesting success. *(1)*
**(a)(iii)** Does mercury level in nesting habitat affect snapping-turtle nest success or nest location? *(1)*
**(a)(iv)** Upstream sites are the control: baseline comparison with mercury-exposed downstream nests. *(1)*
**(a)(v)** Without bank vegetation, less mercury is taken up or filtered, soil near the river erodes, and nests may be placed nearer contaminated ground or in hotter, drier soil, so fewer succeed. *(1)*
**(b)(i)** Persistent mercury bioaccumulates and is a neurotoxin that damages organs, reproduction and survival. *(1)*
**(b)(ii)** It biomagnifies up the food chain, harming top predators and potentially causing trophic cascades and lower diversity. *(1)*
**(b)(iii)** The factory releases inorganic mercury; bacteria in sediment convert it to methylmercury. *(1)*
**(b)(iv)** The map shows nests near the river in Area B failed while those farther away succeeded, supporting the claim that mercury-rich soil near the river reduces success. *(1)*
**(c)** E.g. tilling loosens and erodes soil; monocropping depletes nutrients; fertilizer alters chemistry; irrigation can salinize; heavy machinery compacts soil; legumes add nitrogen. *(1)*

descriptor: Hydraulic fracturing: well-water methane versus distance to a fracking well (graph), how fracking fluid works, a geologic effect, tragedy of the commons, groundwater overuse and saltwater intrusion, and a policy to cut oil use.
solution:
**(a)(i)** Highest methane is 64 mg/L. *(1)*
**(a)(ii)** Methane concentration falls as distance from the fracking well increases (inverse, nonlinear). *(1)*
**(a)(iii)** Any distance of about 1,800-2,200 m, where the curve levels near zero. *(1)*
**(a)(iv)** High-pressure fluid cracks the shale, and sand in the fluid props the fractures open so gas and oil can flow to the well. *(1)*
**(a)(v)** Induced earthquakes or ground subsidence and sinkholes. *(1)*
**(b)(i)** Tragedy of the commons. *(1)*
**(b)(ii)** Falling water tables dry springs and groundwater-fed streams, harm habitats, increase erosion or cause desertification. *(1)*
**(b)(iii)** Pumping lowers the freshwater head in coastal aquifers so seawater flows in (saltwater intrusion), making water too salty to drink. *(1)*
**(c)(i)** Claim: raise vehicle fuel-economy standards, subsidize electric vehicles or transit, invest in renewables, or tax fuel. *(1)*
**(c)(ii)** Justify with a non-climate gain: less smog, particulates and acid rain, or fewer spills and less drilling disturbance. *(1)*

descriptor: Urban heat islands and rooftop solar: cause, a solution and extra benefit, percent change in cell efficiency, change in yearly electricity cost, annual kWh from 30 panels, and seasonal sunlight difference between hemispheres.
solution:
**(a)** Dark pavement and roofs store heat, buildings block wind, there is little shade or evapotranspiration, and vehicles and air conditioners add waste heat. *(1)*
**(b)(i)** E.g. green roofs and more vegetation, reflective light-colored surfaces, or more efficient or less-used heat-producing equipment. *(1)*
**(b)(ii)** Extra benefit: stormwater capture, habitat, cleaner air, insulation or lower energy cost. *(1)*
**(c)(i)** Percent change = (44.5 − 15.9) ÷ 15.9 × 100 ≈ +180%. *(2)*
**(c)(ii)** Change = 12,900 kWh × ($0.13 − $0.11)/kWh = **$258** more per year. *(2)*
**(c)(iii)** 30 panels × 300 W × (1 kW/1,000 W) × 4 h/day × 365 days = 9 kW × 1,460 h = **13,140 kWh/year**. *(2)*
**(d)** June-August the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, so sunlight is more direct and days are longer. *(1)*

descriptor: Gulf of Mexico dead zone: least-extensive watershed land use, how upstream farming and cities feed the zone, effects on marine life and coastal economy, summer growth, and designing a study of riparian buffers on stream nutrients.
solution:
**(a)(i)** Urban land covers the least area. *(1)*
**(a)(ii)** Fertilizer or manure runoff (or sewage) from farms enters rivers, carries nutrients to the Gulf, and fuels algae. *(1)*
**(a)(iii)** Cities release treated or overflow wastewater, and impervious surfaces speed lawn-fertilizer and detergent runoff into the river. *(1)*
**(b)(i)** Algae die and decompose, depleting dissolved oxygen (and block light), so organisms flee or die. *(1)*
**(b)(ii)** Smaller fish catch and fishing income, lower tourism, or higher fuel and consumer costs. *(1)*
**(b)(iii)** Summer brings heavy fertilizer runoff and spring flows, and warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen. *(1)*
**(c)(i)** Hypothesis: stream sites downstream of riparian buffers will have lower nitrate and phosphate than sites without buffers. *(1)*
**(c)(ii)** Control: sites 100 m downstream from areas lacking a vegetation buffer. *(1)*
**(c)(iii)** Another test: turbidity, dissolved oxygen, temperature, fecal coliform, pH, conductivity, BOD or total suspended solids. *(1)*
**(c)(iv)** A feeding operation adds manure nutrients, bacteria, solids or antibiotics that would worsen water quality independent of the buffer, confounding results. *(1)*

descriptor: Lizard counts on Pacific islands with and without mongooses (graph by habitat): richest habitat, mongoose effect, island biogeography, invasive-species harm and control, forest services, effect of sugarcane, monoculture problems and legume rotation.
solution:
**(a)(i)** Clearings and gardens had the most lizards. *(1)*
**(a)(ii)** Inverse: lizard counts are lower where mongooses live than on mongoose-free islands. *(1)*
**(b)** Largest island located close to the mainland has highest species diversity. *(1)*
**(c)(i)** Invasive animals outcompete or prey on natives, cutting biodiversity and disrupting food webs. *(1)*
**(c)(ii)** Claim: biological control, trapping or hunting, manual removal, or chemicals. *(1)*
**(c)(iii)** Justify with a benefit matched to the method, e.g. trapping avoids synthetic chemicals; pesticides act quickly. *(1)*
**(d)(i)** Provisioning service: timber, food or medicine. *(1)*
**(d)(ii)** The graph shows more lizards in cleared land than forest on mongoose-free islands, so converting forest to cane likely increased counts (more food, suitable habitat, fewer predators). *(1)*
**(d)(iii)** Monocultures lower species and genetic diversity, raise pest vulnerability, deplete nutrients and need more inputs. *(1)*
**(e)** Legumes host nitrogen-fixing bacteria, enriching the soil and reducing nitrogen-fertilizer needs. *(1)*

descriptor: Charlotte, North Carolina growth and coal dependence: health effect of coal pollutants, coal-ash disposal problem and clay liners, percent population change 2013-2019, doubling year from a 1.88% rate, annual water use, and cutting outdoor water use.
solution:
**(a)** Coal pollutants cause respiratory disease, heart disease, neurological damage or birth defects. *(1)*
**(b)(i)** Ash leaches toxic metals into groundwater or spills into waterways. *(1)*
**(b)(ii)** Clay is much less permeable than bare soil, so it slows leaching. *(1)*
**(c)(i)** Percent change = (857,425 − 757,278) ÷ 757,278 × 100 ≈ +13.2%. *(2)*
**(c)(ii)** Rule of 70: doubling time = 70 ÷ 1.88 ≈ 37 years; 2019 + 37 = **2056**. *(2)*
**(c)(iii)** 90 gal/person/day × 841,611 people × 365 days ≈ 2.76 × 10¹⁰ gallons. *(2)*
**(d)** Xeriscape or drought-tolerant plants, skip nonessential washing, smart or drip irrigation, rain barrels or gray water, water at night. *(1)*
notes: The coal-ash and coal-health parts are Unit 6 and 8 content; the calculation block is Unit 3.

descriptor: Four-plot trial of three genetically modified bean strains versus unmodified beans on a floodplain: control, research question, less irrigation, runoff and soil-temperature table, fertilizer-use hypothesis, post-burn succession, diversity and recovery, invasive beetle and its control.
solution:
**(a)** Control group: Plot D (unmodified beans). *(1)*
**(b)** Does genetic modification change green-bean yield compared with unmodified beans? *(1)*
**(c)** Less water would lower yields overall, and unmodified beans would likely suffer most if modified types tolerate drought. *(1)*
**(d)** Lowest soil temperature: Plot D (17.6 °C). *(1)*
**(e)** Sediment, phosphorus and nitrogen runoff were all lower from modified-bean plots than from unmodified plot D (e.g. sediment 3.5 vs 0.9-2.4 mg/L). *(1)*
**(f)** Supported: plot B (Type 2) shows far lower P and N runoff than D and still yielded more, so more fertilizer was taken up by plants rather than washed off. *(1)*
**(g)** Secondary succession: pioneer, fast-growing species recolonized soil left intact after the fire. *(1)*
**(h)** More species means a flood removes a smaller share of species and interactions, and diversity includes flood-tolerant types that survive. *(1)*
**(i)** The newcomer could be a generalist or r-selected invader that reproduces quickly and exploits niches opened by the flood in a low-diversity plot. *(1)*
**(j)** Trap or remove beetles, apply pesticide, or introduce a biological control. *(1)*

descriptor: Satellite track of a manatee crossing a shipping channel with water temperatures: temperature range used, why power-plant discharge attracts manatees, harm to other species, seagrass loss effects, an estuary pollution fix, photochemical smog in summer, and fuel-cell car drawbacks.
solution:
**(a)** Most movement occurred in water at about 13-19 °C (read from the diagram). *(1)*
**(b)** The discharge is warm (about 24-26 °C), above the 20 °C survival threshold. *(1)*
**(c)** Warm effluent lowers dissolved oxygen, can exceed other species' tolerance range, and may shift reproductive timing. *(1)*
**(d)(i)** Manatees are herbivores that need much food, have a slow reproductive rate, and are tied to warm water, so seagrass loss means starvation and slow recovery. *(1)*
**(d)(ii)** Less producer biomass, so less energy reaches every higher trophic level. *(1)*
**(e)(i)** Permeable pavement, vegetated buffers, less fertilizer, runoff barriers, or better wastewater treatment. *(1)*
**(e)(ii)** Less nutrient load reduces eutrophication, improves water clarity and biodiversity, supports fisheries or ecotourism. *(1)*
**(f)** Summer has stronger sunlight and heat that speed the reactions of NOₓ and VOCs that form ozone, and trees emit more VOCs. *(1)*
**(g)** Ozone harms plant tissue and photosynthesis, stunts growth and irritates animals' lungs and eyes. *(1)*
**(h)** Hydrogen fuel needs substantial (often fossil) energy to make, is flammable, requires new fueling infrastructure and costly vehicles. *(1)*
notes: Diagram not available as text; the 13-19 degrees C range is taken from the scoring guideline.

descriptor: Crude oil and gold-ore mining: marine impact, a pollutant from burning oil, a personal fuel-saving action and its health benefit, then grams of gold in a deposit, value from 1,000 t, and ore needed for 100,000 phones.
solution:
**(a)** Spills coat or poison marine life, block light, damage wetlands, or noise disrupts animals; fuel CO₂ adds to acidification. *(1)*
**(b)** CO₂, NOₓ, SO₂, particulates, CO or VOCs. *(1)*
**(c)** Walk, bike, use transit, carpool, drive an efficient, hybrid or electric vehicle, or telework. *(1)*
**(d)** Fewer combustion pollutants lowers asthma, COPD and cardiovascular disease; active travel adds fitness. *(1)*
**(e)** 260 × 10⁶ t × 5.0 g/t = 1.3 × 10⁹ g of gold. *(2)*
**(f)** 1,000 t × 5.0 g/t = 5,000 g; × $62.56/g = **$312,800**. *(2)*
**(g)** Gold needed = 0.034 g × 100,000 = 3,400 g; ÷ 5.0 g/t = **680 t** of ore. *(2)*

descriptor: Coal-mine overburden piles restored naturally versus technically (plant-species graph): readings and trends, claim about animal richness, early colonizers, tundra versus forest recovery, then a wheatgrass, wood-chip and bare-soil runoff test, sand effects, and mine-drainage impact and control.
solution:
**(a)** About 8-9 plant species in technically restored piles after 16-25 years (graph reading). *(1)*
**(b)** Plant species richness on spontaneous piles rises with pile age (direct relationship). *(1)*
**(c)** Claim: supports the hypothesis, because more plant species provide more food, shelter and habitat for animals. *(1)*
**(d)** Early colonizers are pioneer or generalist plants that tolerate poor, low-nutrient soil and full sun and spread fast. *(1)*
**(e)** Recovery in tundra would be slower (cold, short season, little rain) and involve tundra species with lower diversity. *(1)*
**(f)** Does ground cover (plants or wood chips) affect the quantity and clarity of runoff? *(1)*
**(g)** Dependent variable: volume of water collected (or its appearance). *(1)*
**(h)** More sand means more infiltration, so less runoff and probably clearer runoff because sand settles quickly. *(1)*
**(i)** Acidic, metal-laden or sediment-rich drainage can exceed tolerance, cause disease or death, or biomagnify metals. *(1)*
**(j)** Plant vegetation, cap waste with soil or lime, divert water, treat drainage, or store waste in basins or under water. *(1)*

descriptor: Spread of Asian carp from the Mississippi basin toward the Great Lakes (map): a water body invaded, distribution change, ecosystem-service impact, control measure and extra benefit, primary consumer, arrow meaning, food-chain effects, blue-pike tragedy of the commons, and aquaculture drawbacks.
solution:
**(a)** Any labeled invaded water body, e.g. Mississippi, Missouri or Ohio River, Lake Erie. *(1)*
**(b)** Carp now occupy a much larger area, having moved up the Mississippi, Missouri and Ohio rivers. *(1)*
**(c)** Possible impacts: reduced fishing or recreation, or changed water quality by displacing native filter feeders. *(1)*
**(d)** Reward fishing for carp, promote eating carp, barriers or electric dispersal, carp-specific deterrents or sound, ballast and bait rules. *(1)*
**(e)** Justify with an added benefit, e.g. new jobs or income, little harm to natives, or protecting food webs. *(1)*
**(f)** Zooplankton (eats algae, the producer). *(1)*
**(g)** Arrows show flow of energy (and matter) from prey to predator. *(1)*
**(h)** Carp compete for plankton, lowering food for fish higher in the chain. *(1)*
**(i)** Blue pike were an open-access shared resource; each fisher maximized catch, and the stock collapsed. *(1)*
**(j)** Aquaculture drawbacks: waste or antibiotic pollution, escapes and disease spread to wild fish, forage-fish feed demand, habitat conversion. *(1)*
notes: Map not available as text; answers for (a)-(b) rely on the guideline.

descriptor: Landfill methane and beef: methane problem, decomposition factors, a fix and extra benefit, then yearly methane from 31.2 million cattle, pasture hectares for one day, and extra people fed if corn replaces beef land.
solution:
**(a)** Methane is a potent greenhouse gas that traps heat, driving warming and sea-level rise. *(1)*
**(b)** Factors: share of organic matter, oxygen and moisture, microbe population, temperature or climate. *(1)*
